file.content:
# Jenkins CI for Gkeyll

This sets up Jenkins (following the pattern used by
[SUNDIALS](https://github.com/llnl/sundials/tree/main/test/jenkins), adapted
for GitHub instead of Bitbucket) to build Gkeyll and run its unit tests on our
own persistent machines any time a pull request into `main` is opened or
updated.

Like `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml`, every build starts from a clean git
checkout and builds its dependencies (`gkylsoft/`) from scratch into its own
Jenkins workspace via `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` — but on our own persistent
hardware instead of an ephemeral GitHub-hosted runner, and it actually
executes the unit tests rather than just building them.

The controller runs on `manauref_lt1` (this laptop). A second workstation can be
added later as an additional build node — see the last section.

## 1. Install Jenkins

```
brew install jenkins-lts
brew services start jenkins-lts
```

This pulls in `openjdk@21` as a dependency. Jenkins listens on
`http://localhost:8080`. Get the initial admin password with:

```
cat ~/.jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
```

(`~/.jenkins` is Homebrew's default `JENKINS_HOME` on macOS — not
`/opt/homebrew/var/lib/jenkins`, despite what some older docs say.) Open
`http://localhost:8080`, paste the password, and install the "suggested
plugins" set when prompted.

## 2. Install additional plugins

Manage Jenkins → Plugins → Available plugins, install:

- **GitHub Branch Source** — lets Jenkins discover branches/PRs on a GitHub
  repo and is the GitHub equivalent of the Bitbucket Branch Source plugin
  SUNDIALS uses.
- **Collapsing Console Sections** (optional) — collapses long build log
  sections for readability, same as SUNDIALS' setup.

## 3. Add a GitHub credential

Jenkins needs read access to `gkeyllorg/gkeyll` to poll for branches and PRs:

1. Create a GitHub Personal Access Token with `repo` scope (Settings →
   Developer settings → Personal access tokens on GitHub).
2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials →
   Add Credentials → kind "GitHub personal access token" (or "Username with
   password", username = your GitHub username, password = the token).

## 4. Label this node `manauref_lt1`

Manage Jenkins → Nodes → "Built-In Node" → Configure → Labels: add
`manauref_lt1`. This is the label the Jenkinsfile's `node('manauref_lt1')` matches.

## 5. Fix this node's `PATH`

Jenkins runs as a `launchd` service (via `brew services`), which does **not**
source your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`) — so it starts with
launchd's bare-bones default `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`) and
can't find Homebrew tools like `cmake`, even though `which cmake` works fine
in your terminal.

Fix this per-node in Jenkins itself (not by editing the launchd plist)
so it works the same way regardless of how each node's agent process is
started — the workstation you add later may be launched over SSH instead of
`brew services`, with a different environment altogether, so a plist edit on
this machine wouldn't help there anyway. Each node keeps its own value here,
which also means this generalizes cleanly once there's more than one node.

Manage Jenkins → Nodes → `manauref_lt1` → Configure → Node Properties → check
"Environment variables" → Add:

- Name: `PATH`
- Value: `/opt/homebrew/bin:/opt/homebrew/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`

(Adjust if your Homebrew prefix or toolchain lives somewhere else.) When you
add the workstation later, give it the equivalent `PATH` for wherever *its*
build tools live.

## 6. Nothing to pre-build

Unlike an earlier version of this setup, the pipeline does **not** assume a
pre-built `gkylsoft/` on this machine. Each build passes
`PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` to `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` and
`machines/configure.macos.sh`, so dependencies are built from scratch inside
that build's own Jenkins workspace — isolated from any manual checkout you
have elsewhere, and safe for concurrent builds of different branches/PRs on
the same node (each gets its own workspace, so its own `gkylsoft/`).

The tradeoff is build time: expect each build to spend several extra minutes
building SuperLU/LuaJIT from source before it even gets to compiling Gkeyll,
same as `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` does on GitHub's runners.

You still need Xcode command line tools / a working C toolchain and `cmake`
on this machine for `mkdeps.macos.sh` to succeed — if you've built Gkeyll
manually before, you already have these.

## 7. Create the multibranch pipeline job

New Item → name it (e.g. `gkeyll`) → **Multibranch Pipeline**.

- **Branch Sources** → Add source → GitHub:
  - Credentials: the one added in step 3.
  - Repository HTTPS URL: `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll`
  - Behaviors: "Discover branches" (at least `main`) and "Discover pull
    requests from origin". Add "Discover pull requests from forks" only if
    external contributors submit PRs from forks.
- **Build Configuration** → Mode: "by Jenkinsfile", Script Path:
  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`.
- **Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers** → check "Periodically if not
  otherwise run" → interval **2 minutes**.

Since this laptop is behind NAT, GitHub can't push a webhook to it. The
periodic scan above is how Jenkins learns about new/updated PRs instead —
every 2 minutes it asks GitHub for changes and kicks off a build if there are
any. This means there's up to a ~2 minute delay before a build starts, which
is an acceptable tradeoff for not having to run a public tunnel (e.g. ngrok)
just to receive webhooks.

Save. Jenkins will scan the repo, find `main` and any open PRs with a
Jenkinsfile, and start building them.

## 8. Adding the second workstation later

1. On the workstation: nothing to install if using SSH launch — Jenkins pushes
   its agent jar over SSH. Make sure Java, a C/C++/Fortran toolchain, and
   `cmake` are present there — `mkdeps` builds everything else from scratch
   per build.
2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New Node → "Permanent Agent" →
   Launch method "Launch agents via SSH", host/credentials for the
   workstation, label it e.g. `workstation-node`.
3. Same as step 5 above: add a `PATH` environment variable under that node's
   Node Properties covering wherever its build tools (`cmake`, compilers,
   MPI, etc.) actually live — don't assume it matches `manauref_lt1`'s value,
   especially if the workstation is Linux.
4. In `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`, add an entry to the `nodes` map, using
   whichever `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts under `machines/` match that
   machine's OS (e.g. Linux instead of macOS):
   ```groovy
   def nodes = [
       'manauref_lt1': ['mkdeps.macos.sh', 'configure.macos.sh'],
       'workstation-node': ['mkdeps.linux.sh', 'configure.linux.cpu.sh'],
   ]
   ```
5. Commit and push. The next PR build will run on both machines in parallel.

## What the pipeline does

Per node, in parallel:

1. `printenv` — for debugging the build environment.
2. `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` — builds `gkylsoft/` from scratch into
   `$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`.
3. `machines/configure.macos.sh` — generates `config.mak` pointing at that
   freshly-built `gkylsoft/`.
4. `make -j3 check` — builds **and runs** all unit tests (`core`, `moments`,
   `vlasov`, `gyrokinetic`, `pkpm`); a failing unit test fails the build.
5. `make -j3 regression` — builds (does not execute) all regression tests,
   matching today's `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` scope. There is no
   automated regression-test runner yet; running a curated subset of
   regression tests is a follow-up.
6. Archives `build/**/*.log` so logs are downloadable from the Jenkins build
   page even on failure.

# -*- makefile-gmake -*-

# include link object list
include ../core/corelinkobjs.mak
include ../moments/momentslinkobjs.mak

SRC_DIRS := zero $(KERNELS_DIR) apps amr
UNIT_DIRS := unit

PREFIX ?= ${HOME}/gkylsoft


CORELLIB := ../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/libg0core.so
CORESLLIB := 
LLIB := ../$(BUILD_DIR)/moments/libg0moments.so
SLLIB := 
SRCS := $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name *.c)
ifdef USING_NVCC
	SRCS += $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name *.cu)
	SRCS += $(shell find $(UNIT_DIRS) -name *.cu)
endif
OBJS := $(SRCS:%=../$(BUILD_DIR)/moments/%.o)
DEPS := $(OBJS:.o=.d)

UNITS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/moments/%,$(wildcard unit/ctest_*.c))
MPI_UNITS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/moments/%,$(wildcard unit/mctest_*.c))
LUA_UNITS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/moments/%,$(wildcard unit/lctest_*.c))

# We need to build CUDA unit-test objects                                                                                                                                            
UNIT_CU_SRCS =
UNIT_CU_OBJS =
ifdef USING_NVCC
    UNIT_CU_SRCS = unit/ctest_wave_geom_cu.cu unit/ctest_wv_euler_cu.cu unit/ctest_wv_maxwell_cu.cu unit/ctest_wv_ten_moment_cu.cu
    UNIT_CU_OBJS = $(UNIT_CU_SRCS:%=../$(BUILD_DIR)/moments/%.o)
endif

REGS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/moments/%,$(wildcard creg/rt_*.c))
AMR_REGS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/moments/%,$(wildcard amr_creg/rt_*.c))

KERN_INC_DIRS = $(shell find $(KERNELS_DIR) -type d)
KERN_INCLUDES = $(addprefix -I,$(KERN_INC_DIRS))
EXT_INCS := -I${MPI_INC_DIR} -I${NCCL_INC_DIR} -I${CUDSS_INC_DIR} -I${LUA_INC_DIR} -I${LAPACK_INC_DIR} -I${SUPERLU_INC_DIR}
INCS := ${EXT_INCS} ${CORE_INCS} -I$(KERNELS_DIR) -Izero -Iapps -Icreg -Iamr $(KERN_INCLUDES)

CORE_LIB_DIR := -L../${BUILD_DIR}/core
CORE_LIB := -lg0core

EXEC_LIB_DIRS = -L${LAPACK_LIB_DIR} -L${SUPERLU_LIB_DIR} -L${MPI_LIB_DIR} -L${NCCL_LIB_DIR} -L${CUDSS_LIB_DIR} -L${LUA_LIB_DIR}

.PHONY: check valcheck
# Run all unit tests
check: unit unit-run ## Build (if needed) and run all unit tests

# Run all unit tests without (re)building them
unit-run: ## Run unit tests without (re)building them
	@cd ..; app=moments; own_log=0; \
	if [ -z "$$GKYL_TEST_LOG" ]; then GKYL_TEST_LOG=$$(mktemp); own_log=1; fi; \
	npass=0; nfail=0; \
	for unit in ${UNITS}; do \
	  tname=$$(basename $$unit); \
	  if ./$$app/$$unit -E; then \
	    npass=$$((npass+1)); echo "PASS $$app: $$tname" >> "$$GKYL_TEST_LOG"; \
	  else \
	    nfail=$$((nfail+1)); echo "FAIL $$app: $$tname" >> "$$GKYL_TEST_LOG"; \
	  fi; \
	done; \
	if [ $$own_log -eq 1 ]; then \
	  echo "==================== $$app test summary ===================="; \
	  echo "Passed: $$npass   Failed: $$nfail"; \
	  if [ $$nfail -gt 0 ]; then \
	    echo "Failed tests:"; grep '^FAIL ' "$$GKYL_TEST_LOG" | sed 's/^FAIL /  /'; rm -f "$$GKYL_TEST_LOG"; exit 1; \
	  else \
	    echo "All $$app unit tests passed."; rm -f "$$GKYL_TEST_LOG"; \
	  fi; \
	fi

valcheck: unit ## Run valgrind on unit test
	cd ../ && $(foreach unit,$(UNITS),valgrind --leak-check=full ./$(patsubst ../%,%,$(unit)) -E 2>./$(patsubst ../%,%,$(unit))_val_err 1>/dev/null;)
	$(foreach unit,$(UNITS),../core/minus/checkval.sh $(unit);)

while [ -n "$1" ]

   --prefix)

      ;;
   --build-openblas)
      [ -n "$value" ] || die "Missing value in flag $key."
      BUILD_OPENBLAS="$value"
      ;;
   --build-superlu)

# Jenkins CI for Gkeyll (SUNDIALS-style), starting on this laptop

## Context

Gkeyll currently only has GitHub-hosted CI (`.github/workflows/mac_build.yml`), which builds unit/regression tests on an ephemeral `macos-latest` runner and never actually *executes* them. You want SUNDIALS' approach instead: a Jenkinsfile checked into the repo, driving a Jenkins controller that runs on **your own hardware** (this laptop now, a second workstation later), so builds happen on real, persistent machines with your existing `gkylsoft/` toolchain already installed — and so tests are actually run, not just compiled.

Repo is `github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll`. SUNDIALS' `test/jenkins/` uses Bitbucket-specific plugins that don't apply here; this plan adapts the same idea (Jenkinsfile in-repo + documented Jenkins setup) to GitHub, using **SCM polling** (no inbound webhook needed since your laptop is behind NAT) and a **Homebrew-installed Jenkins**, per your answers.

Because the Jenkins node is a persistent machine (unlike the ephemeral GitHub Actions runner), dependency builds (`install-deps/mkdeps.sh`) are a one-time manual setup step, not part of every pipeline run — the pipeline just builds Gkeyll and runs tests against the already-installed `gkylsoft/`.

## What I will create in the repo

**`ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`** — declarative pipeline:
- `options { disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true) }` (matches SUNDIALS: a new push/PR update cancels the in-flight build for that branch).
- `stage('Environment')`: `printenv` for debugging (matches SUNDIALS pattern).
- `stage('Build & Test')`: a `parallel` block keyed by node label, e.g. `{'mana-node': { node('mana-node') { ... } }}`. Today only `mana-node` (this laptop) exists; adding the workstation later is just adding another entry to this map with its own label (documented in the README, no Jenkinsfile logic changes needed beyond that one line).
- Steps per node, reusing existing Makefile targets (`Makefile`) exactly as `mac_build.yml` does, but adding the `-run` variants so tests execute, not just build:
  - `make -j3 core-unit && make -j3 core-unit-run`
  - `make -j3 core-regression` (build-only — no regression runner exists yet, matches your chosen scope)
  - same pattern for moments, vlasov, gyrokinetic (unit + unit-run + regression build), and `pkpm-regression` build (pkpm has no separate unit dir per the existing GHA workflow)
  - equivalently, since `make check` already = `unit` + `unit-run` for all modules, the pipeline can just call `make -j3 check` then `make -j3 regression` — simpler and less duplicative than repeating per-module steps; I'll use this form.
- `post`: `always { archiveArtifacts allowEmptyArchive: true, artifacts: 'build/**/*.log' }` so failing test output is retrievable from the Jenkins UI. No Slack/email notification wiring (not requested) — failure is visible via Jenkins build status/GitHub commit status.

**`ci/jenkins/README.md`** — the setup doc, covering exactly the manual steps you'll need to run (Jenkins install/plugins/credentials/job config are GUI/account actions I can't do for you):
1. **Install**: `brew install jenkins-lts` (pulls `openjdk@21`), `brew services start jenkins-lts`, unlock at `http://localhost:8080`.
2. **Plugins**: install suggested set + `GitHub Branch Source` (GitHub equivalent of SUNDIALS' Bitbucket Branch Source) + optionally `Collapsing Console Sections` for readability.
3. **Credentials**: create a GitHub Personal Access Token (`repo` scope, read access to `gkeyllorg/gkeyll`) and add it as a Jenkins credential (Manage Jenkins → Credentials → "GitHub personal access token" kind).
4. **Node label**: add label `mana-node` to the built-in node (Manage Jenkins → Nodes → built-in node → configure), so the Jenkinsfile's `node('mana-node')` resolves.
5. **Job**: New Item → Multibranch Pipeline → GitHub Branch Source pointing at `gkeyllorg/gkeyll`, credential from step 3, Jenkinsfile path `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`. Discover behavior: "Discover pull requests from origin" (add "from forks" only if external contributors submit PRs). Under "Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers," enable "Periodically if not otherwise run" every 2 minutes — this is the SCM-polling substitute for a webhook, and also what discovers new/updated PR branches without any inbound networking.
6. **One-time toolchain setup** (outside Jenkins): confirm `gkylsoft/` is already built on this machine per the existing `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` + `machines/configure.macos.sh` flow — the pipeline assumes this is done already, since re-running `mkdeps.sh` every PR would be slow and is unnecessary on a persistent box.
7. **Adding the workstation later**: install a Jenkins *agent* (not a second controller) on the workstation via SSH launch method (Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New Node, "Launch agents via SSH"), give it its own label (e.g. `workstation-node`), make sure `gkylsoft/` is built there too, then add one entry to the `parallel` map in the Jenkinsfile: `'workstation-node': { node('workstation-node') { ... } }` (same steps, copy-pasted).

## What I will NOT do myself

I can't create the GitHub PAT, click through the Jenkins setup wizard, or configure the multibranch job — those require your GitHub account and Jenkins' web UI. The README will give exact steps/screens so you can do them in a few minutes; I'll write the Jenkinsfile and README, and can help debug once you run through the setup and hit an actual build.

## Verification

- After you finish the manual Jenkins setup, open a test PR against `main` (or push a commit to an existing PR branch) and confirm the multibranch job picks it up within ~2 minutes and runs `test/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`.
- Confirm `make check` failures actually fail the Jenkins build (e.g. temporarily break a unit test assertion on a scratch branch, verify red build, then revert).
- Confirm archived logs are visible/downloadable from the Jenkins build page.

# -*- makefile-gmake -*-

SRC_DIRS := minus $(KERNELS_DIR) zero apps
UNIT_DIRS := unit

PREFIX ?= ${HOME}/gkylsoft


LLIB := ../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/libg0core.so
SLLIB := 
SRCS := $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name *.c)
ifdef USING_NVCC
	SRCS += $(shell find $(SRC_DIRS) -name *.cu)
	SRCS += $(shell find $(UNIT_DIRS) -name *.cu)
endif
OBJS := $(SRCS:%=../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/%.o)
DEPS := $(OBJS:.o=.d)

UNITS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/core/%,$(wildcard unit/ctest_*.c))
MPI_UNITS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/core/%,$(wildcard unit/mctest_*.c))
LUA_UNITS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/core/%,$(wildcard unit/lctest_*.c))

# We need to build CUDA unit-test objects                                                                                                                                            
UNIT_CU_SRCS =
UNIT_CU_OBJS =
ifdef USING_NVCC
    UNIT_CU_SRCS = unit/ctest_cusolver.cu unit/ctest_alloc_cu.cu unit/ctest_basis_cu.cu unit/ctest_array_cu.cu unit/ctest_range_cu.cu unit/ctest_rect_grid_cu.cu unit/ctest_struct_of_arrays_cu.cu
ifdef USING_CUDSS
    UNIT_CU_SRCS += unit/ctest_cudss.cu
endif
    UNIT_CU_OBJS = $(UNIT_CU_SRCS:%=../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/%.o)
endif

REGS := $(patsubst %.c,../${BUILD_DIR}/core/%,$(wildcard creg/rt_*.c))

KERN_INC_DIRS = $(shell find $(KERNELS_DIR) -type d)
KERN_INCLUDES = $(addprefix -I,$(KERN_INC_DIRS))
EXT_INCS := -I${MPI_INC_DIR} -I${NCCL_INC_DIR} -I${CUDSS_INC_DIR} -I${LUA_INC_DIR} -I${LAPACK_INC_DIR} -I${SUPERLU_INC_DIR}
INCS := ${EXT_INCS} -Iminus -Iminus/STC/include -Izero -Iapps $(KERN_INCLUDES) -Ilua/Comm -Ilua/Tool

EXEC_LIB_DIRS = -L${LAPACK_LIB_DIR} -L${SUPERLU_LIB_DIR} -L${MPI_LIB_DIR} -L${NCCL_LIB_DIR} -L${CUDSS_LIB_DIR} -L${LUA_LIB_DIR}
EXEC_EXT_LIBS = ${LAPACK_LIBS} ${SUPERLU_LIBS} ${CUDA_LIBS} ${MPI_RPATH} ${MPI_LIBS} ${NCCL_LIBS} ${CUDSS_RPATH} ${CUDSS_LIBS} ${LUA_RPATH} ${LUA_LIBS} -lm -lpthread -ldl
EXEC_LIBS = -L../${BUILD_DIR}/core ${LLIB} ${SLLIB} ${EXEC_EXT_LIBS}

LDFLAGS += -Wl,-rpath,./${BUILD_DIR}/core
LDFLAGS += -Wl,-rpath,../${BUILD_DIR}/core

unit: ${LLIB} ${SLLIB} $(UNITS) ${MPI_UNITS} ${LUA_UNITS} ## Build unit tests
regression: ${LLIB} ${SLLIB} ${REGS} ## Build regression tests

.PHONY: all
all: $(LLIB) ## Build all targets
.DEFAULT_GOAL := all

# SQLITE needs special flags
../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/minus/sqlite3.c.o: minus/sqlite3.c
	$(MKDIR_P) $(dir $@)
	$(CC) $(SQL_CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

# c -> o files
../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/%.c.o: %.c
	$(MKDIR_P) $(dir $@)
	$(CC) -c $(CFLAGS) $(ARCH_FLAGS) $(INCS) $< -o $@

# Build commands for CUDA source                                                                                                                                                     
../$(BUILD_DIR)/core/%.cu.o: %.cu
	$(MKDIR_P) $(dir $@)
	$(CC) -c $(CFLAGS) $(NVCC_FLAGS) $(INCS) $< -o $@

content.text:
Confirmed the root cause. In `core/Makefile-core`, `unit: ${LLIB} ...` and `regression: ${LLIB} ...` — so `core-unit`'s recipe (`cd core && make -f Makefile-core unit`) builds `libg0core.so` itself, just like the top-level `core:` target's recipe does. But in the top-level `Makefile`, `core-unit` and `core-regression` have **no prerequisites at all**, unlike every other module (`moments-unit: moments core-unit`, `vlasov-unit: vlasov moments-unit`, etc., which correctly depend on their own base target).

So when `make -j3` builds `moments-unit: moments core-unit`, it sees `moments` (which needs `core`) and `core-unit` (which needs nothing) as independent, parallelizable prerequisites — and runs two concurrent `cd core && make -f Makefile-core ...` sub-processes that both try to build `libg0core.so`, racing on the same object files/link step. That's the undefined-symbol failure.

Fix: add `core` as an explicit prerequisite to `core-unit` and `core-regression`, matching the pattern already used everywhere else.

content.text:
Fixed. The dry-run confirms `core`'s recipe now runs to completion before `core-unit`'s recipe starts, instead of racing.

**Root cause**: in the top-level `Makefile`, `core-unit` and `core-regression` had no prerequisites, unlike every other module's `-unit`/`-regression` target (e.g. `moments-unit: moments core-unit`), which properly chain back to their base build target. Since `core/Makefile-core`'s own `unit`/`regression` targets build `libg0core.so` themselves (`unit: ${LLIB} ...`), and the top-level `core:` target's recipe does the same recursive `make -f Makefile-core` call, under `-j3` two separate recursive sub-makes could end up compiling/linking `core/`'s sources into `libg0core.so` concurrently — corrupting the object files and producing the undefined-symbol linker errors you saw (`_gkyl_register_distribution_moment_types`, `_glua_tbl_iget_integer`, etc., which are real symbols, just missing because the .so got linked mid-race).

**Fix**: added `core` as an explicit prerequisite to `core-unit` and `core-regression`, matching the existing `core-check: core` pattern already used elsewhere in the file — a one-line-per-target change to `Makefile`.

This should resolve the linker failure on the next Jenkins build. Push this commit (or amend it into your PR branch) and re-trigger.

# Jenkins CI for Gkeyll

This sets up Jenkins (following the pattern used by
[SUNDIALS](https://github.com/llnl/sundials/tree/main/test/jenkins), adapted
for GitHub instead of Bitbucket) to build Gkeyll and run its unit tests on our
own persistent machines any time a pull request into `main` is opened or
updated.

Like `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml`, every build starts from a clean git
checkout and builds its dependencies (`gkylsoft/`) from scratch into its own
Jenkins workspace via `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` — but on our own persistent
hardware instead of an ephemeral GitHub-hosted runner, and it actually
executes the unit tests rather than just building them.

The controller runs on `manauref_lt1` (this laptop). A second workstation can be
added later as an additional build node — see the last section.

## 1. Install Jenkins

```
brew install jenkins-lts
brew services start jenkins-lts
```

This pulls in `openjdk@21` as a dependency. Jenkins listens on
`http://localhost:8080`. Get the initial admin password with:

```
cat ~/.jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
```

(`~/.jenkins` is Homebrew's default `JENKINS_HOME` on macOS — not
`/opt/homebrew/var/lib/jenkins`, despite what some older docs say.) Open
`http://localhost:8080`, paste the password, and install the "suggested
plugins" set when prompted.

## 2. Install additional plugins

Manage Jenkins → Plugins → Available plugins, install:

- **GitHub Branch Source** — lets Jenkins discover branches/PRs on a GitHub
  repo and is the GitHub equivalent of the Bitbucket Branch Source plugin
  SUNDIALS uses.
- **Collapsing Console Sections** (optional) — collapses long build log
  sections for readability, same as SUNDIALS' setup.

## 3. Add a GitHub credential

Jenkins needs read access to `gkeyllorg/gkeyll` to poll for branches and PRs:

1. Create a GitHub Personal Access Token with `repo` scope (Settings →
   Developer settings → Personal access tokens on GitHub).
2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials →
   Add Credentials → kind "GitHub personal access token" (or "Username with
   password", username = your GitHub username, password = the token).

## 4. Label this node `manauref_lt1`

Manage Jenkins → Nodes → "Built-In Node" → Configure → Labels: add
`manauref_lt1`. This is the label the Jenkinsfile's `node('manauref_lt1')` matches.

## 5. Fix this node's `PATH`

Jenkins runs as a `launchd` service (via `brew services`), which does **not**
source your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`) — so it starts with
launchd's bare-bones default `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`) and
can't find Homebrew tools like `cmake`, even though `which cmake` works fine
in your terminal.

Fix this per-node in Jenkins itself (not by editing the launchd plist)
so it works the same way regardless of how each node's agent process is
started — the workstation you add later may be launched over SSH instead of
`brew services`, with a different environment altogether, so a plist edit on
this machine wouldn't help there anyway. Each node keeps its own value here,
which also means this generalizes cleanly once there's more than one node.

Manage Jenkins → Nodes → `manauref_lt1` → Configure → Node Properties → check
"Environment variables" → Add:

- Name: `PATH`
- Value: `/opt/homebrew/bin:/opt/homebrew/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`

(Adjust if your Homebrew prefix or toolchain lives somewhere else.) When you
add the workstation later, give it the equivalent `PATH` for wherever *its*
build tools live.

## 6. Nothing to pre-build

Unlike an earlier version of this setup, the pipeline does **not** assume a
pre-built `gkylsoft/` on this machine. Each build passes
`PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` to `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` and
`machines/configure.macos.sh`, so dependencies are built from scratch inside
that build's own Jenkins workspace — isolated from any manual checkout you
have elsewhere, and safe for concurrent builds of different branches/PRs on
the same node (each gets its own workspace, so its own `gkylsoft/`).

The tradeoff is build time: expect each build to spend several extra minutes
building SuperLU/LuaJIT from source before it even gets to compiling Gkeyll,
same as `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` does on GitHub's runners.

You still need Xcode command line tools / a working C toolchain and `cmake`
on this machine for `mkdeps.macos.sh` to succeed — if you've built Gkeyll
manually before, you already have these.

## 7. Create the multibranch pipeline job

New Item → name it (e.g. `gkeyll`) → **Multibranch Pipeline**.

- **Branch Sources** → Add source → GitHub:
  - Credentials: the one added in step 3.
  - Repository HTTPS URL: `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll`
  - Behaviors: "Discover branches" (at least `main`) and "Discover pull
    requests from origin". Add "Discover pull requests from forks" only if
    external contributors submit PRs from forks.
- **Build Configuration** → Mode: "by Jenkinsfile", Script Path:
  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`.
- **Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers** → check "Periodically if not
  otherwise run" → interval **2 minutes**.

Since this laptop is behind NAT, GitHub can't push a webhook to it. The
periodic scan above is how Jenkins learns about new/updated PRs instead —
every 2 minutes it asks GitHub for changes and kicks off a build if there are
any. This means there's up to a ~2 minute delay before a build starts, which
is an acceptable tradeoff for not having to run a public tunnel (e.g. ngrok)
just to receive webhooks.

Save. Jenkins will scan the repo, find `main` and any open PRs with a
Jenkinsfile, and start building them.

## 8. Adding the second workstation later

1. On the workstation: nothing to install if using SSH launch — Jenkins pushes
   its agent jar over SSH. Make sure Java, a C/C++/Fortran toolchain, and
   `cmake` are present there — `mkdeps` builds everything else from scratch
   per build.
2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New Node → "Permanent Agent" →
   Launch method "Launch agents via SSH", host/credentials for the
   workstation, label it e.g. `workstation-node`.
3. Same as step 5 above: add a `PATH` environment variable under that node's
   Node Properties covering wherever its build tools (`cmake`, compilers,
   MPI, etc.) actually live — don't assume it matches `manauref_lt1`'s value,
   especially if the workstation is Linux.
4. In `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`, add an entry to the `nodes` map, using
   whichever `mkdeps`/`configure` scripts under `machines/` match that
   machine's OS (e.g. Linux instead of macOS):
   ```groovy
   def nodes = [
       'manauref_lt1': ['mkdeps.macos.sh', 'configure.macos.sh'],
       'workstation-node': ['mkdeps.linux.sh', 'configure.linux.cpu.sh'],
   ]
   ```
5. Commit and push. The next PR build will run on both machines in parallel.

## What the pipeline does

Per node, in parallel:

1. `printenv` — for debugging the build environment.
2. `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` — builds `gkylsoft/` from scratch into
   `$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft`.
3. `machines/configure.macos.sh` — generates `config.mak` pointing at that
   freshly-built `gkylsoft/`.
4. `make -j3 check` — builds **and runs** all unit tests (`core`, `moments`,
   `vlasov`, `gyrokinetic`, `pkpm`); a failing unit test fails the build.
5. `make -j3 regression` — builds (does not execute) all regression tests,
   matching today's `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` scope. There is no
   automated regression-test runner yet; running a curated subset of
   regression tests is a follow-up.
6. Archives `build/**/*.log` so logs are downloadable from the Jenkins build
   page even on failure.

#!/bin/bash

source ./build-opts.sh

# Edit to suite your system
PREFIX=$GKYLSOFT/superlu-7.0.0
# Location where dependency sources will be downloaded
DEP_SOURCES=$GKYLSOFT/dep_src/

mkdir -p $DEP_SOURCES
cd $DEP_SOURCES

if [ "$DOWNLOAD_PKGS" = "yes" ]
then
    echo "Downloading SuperLU .."
    # delete old checkout and builds
    rm -rf superlu-*
    curl -L https://github.com/xiaoyeli/superlu/archive/refs/tags/v7.0.1.tar.gz > superlu-7.0.1.tar.gz
fi

if [ "$BUILD_PKGS" = "yes" ]
then
    echo "Building SuperLU .."
    gunzip -f superlu-7.0.1.tar.gz
    tar xvf superlu-7.0.1.tar

    cd superlu-7.0.1
    mkdir build
    cd build

    # configure build
    cmake .. -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-g -O3 -fPIC" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PREFIX -DCMAKE_INSTALL_LIBDIR=lib -Denable_tests=NO -Denable_internal_blaslib=NO -DXSDK_ENABLE_Fortran=NO -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=$CC -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$CXX -DMPI_C_COMPILER=$MPICC -DMPI_CXX_COMPILER=$MPICXX

    # build and install
    make -j 32 VERBOSE=1
    make install

    # soft-link 
    ln -sfn $PREFIX $GKYLSOFT/superlu
fi

# Jenkins CI for Gkeyll

This sets up Jenkins (following the pattern used by
[SUNDIALS](https://github.com/llnl/sundials/tree/main/test/jenkins), adapted
for GitHub instead of Bitbucket) to build Gkeyll and run its unit tests on our
own persistent machines any time a pull request into `main` is opened or
updated.

Like `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml`, every build starts from a clean git
checkout and builds its dependencies (`gkylsoft/`) from scratch into its own
Jenkins workspace via `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` — but on our own persistent
hardware instead of an ephemeral GitHub-hosted runner, and it actually
executes the unit tests rather than just building them.

The controller runs on `manauref_lt1` (this laptop). A second workstation can be
added later as an additional build node — see the last section.

## 1. Install Jenkins

```
brew install jenkins-lts
brew services start jenkins-lts
```

This pulls in `openjdk@21` as a dependency. Jenkins listens on
`http://localhost:8080`. Get the initial admin password with:

```
cat ~/.jenkins/secrets/initialAdminPassword
```

(`~/.jenkins` is Homebrew's default `JENKINS_HOME` on macOS — not
`/opt/homebrew/var/lib/jenkins`, despite what some older docs say.) Open
`http://localhost:8080`, paste the password, and install the "suggested
plugins" set when prompted.

## 2. Install additional plugins

Manage Jenkins → Plugins → Available plugins, install:

- **GitHub Branch Source** — lets Jenkins discover branches/PRs on a GitHub
  repo and is the GitHub equivalent of the Bitbucket Branch Source plugin
  SUNDIALS uses.
- **Collapsing Console Sections** (optional) — collapses long build log
  sections for readability, same as SUNDIALS' setup.

## 3. Add a GitHub credential

Jenkins needs read access to `gkeyllorg/gkeyll` to poll for branches and PRs:

1. Create a GitHub Personal Access Token with `repo` scope (Settings →
   Developer settings → Personal access tokens on GitHub).
2. In Jenkins: Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials →
   Add Credentials → kind "GitHub personal access token" (or "Username with
   password", username = your GitHub username, password = the token).

## 4. Label this node `manauref_lt1`

Manage Jenkins → Nodes → "Built-In Node" → Configure → Labels: add
`manauref_lt1`. This is the label the Jenkinsfile's `node('manauref_lt1')` matches.

## 5. Fix this node's `PATH`

Jenkins runs as a `launchd` service (via `brew services`), which does **not**
source your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.zprofile`) — so it starts with
launchd's bare-bones default `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`) and
can't find Homebrew tools like `cmake`, even though `which cmake` works fine
in your terminal.

Fix this per-node in Jenkins itself (not by editing the launchd plist)
so it works the same way regardless of how each node's agent process is
started — the workstation you add later may be launched over SSH instead of
`brew services`, with a different environment altogether, so a plist edit on
this machine wouldn't help there anyway. Each node keeps its own value here,
which also means this generalizes cleanly once there's more than one node.

Manage Jenkins → Nodes → `manauref_lt1` → Configure → Node Properties → check
"Environment variables" → Add:

- Name: `PATH`
- Value: `/opt/homebrew/bin:/opt/homebrew/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`

(Adjust if your Homebrew prefix or toolchain lives somewhere else.) When you
add the workstation later, give it the equivalent `PATH` for wherever *its*
build tools live.

## 6. Nothing to pre-build

Unlike an earlier version of this setup, the pipeline does **not** assume a
pre-built `gkylsoft/` on this machine. Each build passes
`PREFIX=$WORKSPACE/gkylsoft` to `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` and
`machines/configure.macos.sh`, so dependencies are built from scratch inside
that build's own Jenkins workspace — isolated from any manual checkout you
have elsewhere, and safe for concurrent builds of different branches/PRs on
the same node (each gets its own workspace, so its own `gkylsoft/`).

The tradeoff is build time: expect each build to spend several extra minutes
building SuperLU/LuaJIT from source before it even gets to compiling Gkeyll,
same as `.github/workflows/mac_build.yml` does on GitHub's runners.

You still need Xcode command line tools / a working C toolchain and `cmake`
on this machine for `mkdeps.macos.sh` to succeed — if you've built Gkeyll
manually before, you already have these.

## 7. Create the multibranch pipeline job

New Item → name it (e.g. `gkeyll`) → **Multibranch Pipeline**.

- **Branch Sources** → Add source → GitHub:
  - Credentials: the one added in step 3.
  - Repository HTTPS URL: `https://github.com/gkeyllorg/gkeyll`
  - Behaviors: "Discover branches" (at least `main`) and "Discover pull
    requests from origin". Add "Discover pull requests from forks" only if
    external contributors submit PRs from forks.
- **Build Configuration** → Mode: "by Jenkinsfile", Script Path:
  `ci/jenkins/Jenkinsfile`.
- **Scan Multibranch Pipeline Triggers** → check "Periodically if not
  otherwise run" → interval **2 minutes**.

Since this laptop is behind NAT, GitHub can't push a webhook to it. The
periodic scan above is how Jenkins learns about new/updated PRs instead —
every 2 minutes it asks GitHub for changes and kicks off a build if there are
any. This means there's up to a ~2 minute delay before a build starts, which
is an acceptable tradeoff for not having to run a public tunnel (e.g. ngrok)
just to receive webhooks.

message.content: Just out of curiosity, is it possible to add --build-adas=yes to the machine file Jenkins runs, but not to the machine file committed in the repo?

content.text:
Yes — a couple of ways: (1) have `machines/mkdeps.macos.sh` forward extra args (e.g. `./mkdeps.sh ... "$@"`) so the Jenkinsfile appends `--build-adas=yes` itself without touching the committed defaults, or (2) keep a separate `machines/mkdeps.macos.ci.sh` that Jenkins points at instead.

I'd lean against it here, though: `--build-adas=yes` isn't a CI-only quirk — any developer running `make check` on gyrokinetic locally with the plain script would hit the same two test failures, since the tests genuinely need that data regardless of who's building. Keeping it in the shared script means Jenkins and manual dev builds behave the same way and nobody has to remember an extra flag; a CI-only override would just be one more thing to explain in the README to future you.
